Antagonize

an-TAG-uh-nyze · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To antagonize to cause someone to become hostile.

Without meaning to, the new manager antagonized the entire warehouse crew by canceling their usual break schedule on his first day.

Worked Example

The columnist seemed to enjoy antagonizing his readers, writing one deliberately provocative opinion piece after another just to watch the angry comments pour in.

Antagonize means to cause someone to become hostile -- the columnist isn't confronting readers directly, but his writing provokes hostility in them anyway.

How Antagonize Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

rile

rile: to make someone annoyed or angry

irritate

irritate: to make someone impatient or angry

Antonyms

soothe

soothe: to calm or comfort someone

reassure

reassure: to restore someone's confidence and ease their worry

How Strong Is It? — annoy → antagonize → incense

annoy vs. antagonize

annoy vs. antagonize: Annoy describes causing mild irritation, without necessarily provoking real hostility.

incense vs. antagonize

incense vs. antagonize: Incense means to make someone extremely angry -- a stronger reaction than the hostility caused by antagonizing them.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ant-

prefix — ant-: a variant of anti-, meaning against (Greek)

root — agon

root — agon: contest, struggle (Greek agon)

suffix — -ize

suffix — -ize: to cause to become, to make (Greek -izein)

Put it together

Put it together: Antagonize comes from Greek anti- ('against') + agon ('contest, struggle') + -izein ('to make') -- literally 'to make into a struggle against.'

Use the root in a new word: agony

Use the root in a new word: agony: After the marathon, she collapsed in agony, her legs completely spent.

Root Check

Word Choice

Antagonize describes causing hostility in someone, often without a direct face-to-face confrontation -- unlike accost (an aggressive physical confrontation) or upbraid (a direct scolding). It shares its Greek root (agon, 'contest, struggle') with antagonist, a word taught in this course's very first unit on this same theme.
